analysis.one_liner: Caps insulin out-of-pocket costs at $35 a month and waives deductibles for insulin in private health plans.
analysis.headline: The bill was introduced in November 2025 and sent to three House committees, where it has had no further action.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill requires private health plans — employer plans and individual insurance bought on or off the marketplaces — to cover at least one insulin of every type and dosage form with no deductible and cost-sharing capped at $35 for a 30-day supply, or 25% of the plan's net price if that's cheaper. It also forces catastrophic plans to cover insulin before the enrollee has hit their huge annual deductible, and makes insulin cost-sharing count toward deductibles and out-of-pocket maximums. It does not set the price drug makers can charge; it only limits what the patient pays out of pocket.
analysis.who_benefits: People who use insulin and have private insurance — through an employer or bought individually. They would no longer pay a deductible before insulin coverage starts and would pay at most $35 per 30-day supply (or 25% of the plan's net insulin price if lower). People with high-deductible or catastrophic plans benefit most, since insulin would be covered up front instead of after thousands of dollars in spending.

how_it_helps.text: Group and individual health plans must cover selected insulin products with no deductible and cost-sharing capped at $35 per 30-day supply, or 25% of the plan's net negotiated price if lower [S2].
Plans must cover at least one product of each insulin type (rapid-, short-, intermediate-, long-, ultra long-acting, and premixed) and each dosage form (vial, pump, inhaler) when available [S2].
Catastrophic plans must cover selected insulin products before the enrollee has reached the annual deductible limit, so people with catastrophic coverage get protected insulin pricing up front [S2].
Cost-sharing paid for insulin counts toward deductibles and out-of-pocket maximums, so insulin spending still moves people toward full coverage [S2].

analysis.who_pays: Health plans and the employers and insurers behind them absorb the difference between what patients used to pay and the $35 cap, which could show up as somewhat higher premiums spread across everyone with the plan. Pharmacy benefit managers may capture fewer price concessions on insulin. Drug makers face no new price limit, so the underlying list price of insulin is unchanged.
analysis.who_pays_short: Health plans, employers, and pharmacy benefit managers

drawbacks.text: The bill caps only what the patient pays out of pocket — it puts no limit on the price manufacturers can charge, so the underlying cost of insulin is untouched and the difference is shifted into premiums and plan costs [S2].
The cap applies only to the plan's 'selected insulin products'; plans can still charge higher cost-sharing on any other insulin products not on that list [S2].
Plans can impose higher cost-sharing or deny coverage for insulin delivered by an out-of-network provider [S2].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The patient-side benefit is real and immediate: no deductible and a $35 monthly ceiling for insulin users, which for people on high-deductible plans can be the difference between rationing insulin and taking it as prescribed. The honest cost is that the money has to come from somewhere — plans, employers, and eventually premiums — and because the bill does not cap manufacturer prices, it leaves the biggest driver of insulin costs alone. It is a targeted patient-protection bill, not a price fix.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced in late November 2025 and referred to three House committees, and none of them has taken it up since.

narrative.text: Rep. Angie Craig introduced the Affordable Insulin Now Act on November 21, 2025 [S1].
The bill was referred to the Energy and Commerce, Ways and Means, and Education and Workforce Committees; no committee has acted and no vote has been scheduled [S4].
All 11 cosponsors are House Democrats, and no further action has occurred since referral [S3].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: So far, nothing has changed: health plans, employers, and pharmacy benefit managers keep the current cost-sharing arrangements, and insulin users with private coverage keep paying whatever their plans charge.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: No one has moved; current plan cost-sharing continues

against.name: House committees of jurisdiction (Energy and Commerce, Ways and Means, Education and Workforce)
against.role: Committees to which the bill was referred
against.what_they_did: Received the bill by referral in November 2025 and have taken no action — no hearing, markup, or vote scheduled [S4].

sides.party_line_note: The sponsor and all 11 cosponsors are Democrats; no Republican has signed on, and the bill sits untouched in committees of a Republican-controlled House [S3].

industries.note: Plans must cover selected insulin up front and absorb any patient cost above $35 per month, which pressures premiums. But plans stay the gatekeepers: they choose which insulin products count, can exclude non-selected insulins, and can charge more for out-of-network supply [S2].
The cap is measured against the plan's net price after all price concessions, including those captured by PBMs, so PBM middleman economics on insulin come under the cap's math [S2].

The bill puts no ceiling on what manufacturers can charge, so their list prices are untouched; they keep selling insulin through private plans with plans and patients financing the cost-sharing cap [S2].

analysis.trajectory: With no committee action since November and no Republican cosponsors, the bill is likely to sit until it expires with the 119th Congress, as most bills do; a version of this same proposal did pass the House in 2022, so insulin pricing could re-enter the agenda and revive it.
